The test image shows a cross-sectioned corn stalk/node with:
- Very dark black outer rind ring
- White/cream colored pith interior
- White mold/mycelium visible on the cut surface
- Some small yellowish structures visible on the pith face
- Brownish fibrous material at top

Top candidates: **Anthracnose_stalk_rot** (shiny black rind), **Diplodia_stalk_rot** (white mold + black pycnidia), **Bacterial_stalk_rot** (soft rot at nodes).

Let me view reference images for the top candidates in parallel.
The Anthracnose stalk rot reference shows the characteristic shiny black rind that matches the test image. Let me view a few more to confirm.

The Physoderma stalk rot reference (bottom-left) shows a very similar cross-section at a node with dark outer ring and lighter pith interior — closely matching the test image. Let me do one more comparison.

The ear rot references don't match — the test image is clearly a stalk cross-section, not an ear.

**Final analysis:**

- **Test image**: Cross-section of a corn stalk at a **node**, showing very dark black outer ring (node tissue), white/cream inner pith with white mold/mycelium, and small yellowish structures on the cut face.

- **Physoderma_stalk_rot** is the best match: "Plants break at the first or second node, which appear **black** with possible pith rot." The Physoderma reference image (bottom-left) showed an almost identical cross-section at a node with a dark outer ring and lighter interior.

- **Anthracnose_stalk_rot** was a strong runner-up due to "distinctive shiny black discoloration of the stalk rind," but Anthracnose typically shows more diffuse black rind along the entire stalk, whereas the blackness in the test image is concentrated specifically at the node — the hallmark of Physoderma stalk rot.
